activities.caption: rebuild the two seams that split classical physics
activities.name: qfSeamsOrder

config.prompt: Assemble the story of the first crack, in order:
items: Classical electromagnetism predicts any warm object radiates infinite energy at short wavelengths — the ultraviolet catastrophe: every oven a death ray
Planck fixes the arithmetic (1900) with a reluctant assumption: matter exchanges energy with light in discrete lumps of E = hf
He calls it a 'mathematical trick' — but it is the price of admission to the quantum world
Einstein — not for relativity but for this — takes the lumps literally in the photoelectric effect and wins the 1921 Nobel Prize
config.why: One constant, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, governs the granularity — and the classical continuum is what you see when the grains are too fine to notice.

activities.anchor: Shine light on a metal; electrons come out
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the too-red lamp
activities.name: qfRedPredict

config.q: Light below the threshold frequency shines on a metal. You crank the intensity up a thousandfold. What happens?
choices: Electrons emerge after a delay, once they have slowly accumulated enough energy
Still nothing — a trillion dim photons cannot stack, because they arrive one at a time
Electrons emerge immediately, but with almost no kinetic energy
The threshold frequency drops until electrons can escape
config.why: Classical physics predicted delay and intensity-rescue; the experiments said the opposite. One photon, one electron — brightness controls only how many electrons emerge, never whether any do.

activities.caption: guess the magnitude — a photon's budget in eV
activities.name: qfPhotonEst

config.prompt: Using the eV shortcut (photon energy ≈ 1240 / wavelength in nm): how many eV does one red 650 nm photon carry?
config.why: 1240/650 ≈ 1.9 eV — short by 0.4 eV against sodium's 2.28 eV work function, so nothing happens regardless of brightness. Blue 450 nm carries 2.76 eV and ejects electrons at 0.48 eV.
config.context: The same shortcut runs semiconductors, solar cells and the spectroscopy lessons.

activities.anchor: beams through two slits should paint two stripes
activities.caption: pair each double-slit fact with its meaning
activities.name: qfSlitMatch

config.prompt: One particle at a time — pair each fact with its meaning:

pairs.right: every particle with momentum p has a wavelength — not a small one: a 50 eV electron's is ≈ 0.17 nm

pairs.left: electrons fired one at a time
pairs.right: each lands as a single dot, apparently random — yet thousands accumulate into fringes
interference demonstrated for molecules, not just fundmental particles

pairs.left: detecting which slit the electron used
pairs.right: the fringes vanish; the pattern becomes two stripes

config.why: Each particle explores both paths and the two amplitudes add — sometimes reinforcing, sometimes cancelling. Davisson and Germer confirmed the diffraction off nickel crystals in 1927.

activities.anchor: a gentler which-path detector would keep the fringes
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's lab notes
activities.name: qfDetectorSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's double-slit lab notes is wrong — click it:
lines: Fire the electrons one at a time: single dots, and the fringes build up dot by dot.
De Broglie's λ = h/p fixes the electron's wavelength — about 0.17 nm at 50 eV.
A gentler probe would keep the fringes intact, since it transfers less momentum to the electron.
Any interaction that irreversibly records the path destroys the interference, however gentle.
The two amplitudes must remain indistinguishable for interference to survive.
config.correction: Knowledge itself is not the mechanism and gentleness cannot save the fringes: any which-path record entangles the electron with the detector and decoheres the superposition — information, not force, does the destroying.
config.why: Classical observation means disturbance; quantum measurement-sensitivity is deeper — it is the theory's central postulate wearing experimental clothes.

activities.caption: true or false — the energy–time cousin
activities.name: qfEnergyTimeJudge

statements.s: ΔE · Δt ≥ ħ/2 has a measurement-disturbance reading, just like Δx · Δp.
statements.why: It has no measurement-disturbance reading at all — it says short-lived states have uncertain energy.

statements.s: An excited atom decaying after ~10 ns has a spectral line broadened by about 10⁻⁷ eV.
statements.why: The natural linewidth — the fact spectroscopists exploit to measure lifetimes.

statements.s: Virtual particles borrow energy for a time the inequality permits.
statements.why: The accounting that makes quantum field theory work.

statements.s: Better instruments could beat the Δx · Δp limit.
statements.why: The disturbance story would predict that, and they cannot — it is Fourier mathematics: localising a wave forces momentum spread.

activities.caption: walk the two-tier rule for measurement
activities.name: qfTwoTierBranch

config.root: An electron flies toward a screen, unmeasured. Walk the two-tier structure of quantum prediction.

start.text: While it flies, what is the electron's story?

choices.label: A wave evolving smoothly and deterministically under the Schrödinger equation
A dot already waiting at its landing spot

nopreset.text: That is the picture the theory refuses to give: no equation governs which outcome occurs — only the statistics.

choices.label: So the dot appears — what is predicted?

dot.text: The dot appears. What does the theory predict about this individual event?

choices.label: Exactly where it lands, if the wavefunction is known well enough
Nothing individually — only Born-rule probabilities over many runs

refusal.text: That is the refusal: individual events are unpredictable. The electron's magnetic moment matches theory to one part in a trillion — in the statistics.

statistics.text: Between measurements the wave evolves smoothly again — deterministic evolution, then a probabilistic jump no equation governs. Whether that jump is a complete description of nature is the measurement problem, the page's open wound.

config.why: Quantum mechanics predicts the statistics of outcomes with spectacular precision while declining to predict individual events — the two-tier structure is the theory's shape.

activities.caption: which curve is the ground-state probability cloud?
activities.name: qfPsiTrace

config.prompt: An electron trapped in a box from x = 0 to 1. Which curve is its ground-state probability density |ψ|²?
config.why: The Born rule: probability density is the squared magnitude — no sign, peak at the centre, zero at the walls. A standing wave in a box plays discrete notes, which is what makes orbitals discrete.
